title: Nala and Damayanti
hook: Nala carries a snake out of a forest fire, and its bite hides him from the world
carry: notice the words you say at day's end

segments.voice: Yesterday the story of Nala and Damayanti followed her alone, asking a mountain and an Ashoka tree where he'd gone. Your line was keep asking the one question that matters. What question did you keep asking? Day seven hundred ninety-three.

A voice in a forest fire. Nala, wandering alone after leaving Damayanti, hears someone calling his name out of the flames. Come quickly, Nala. He follows the voice and finds, curled in the fire, a great serpent. It's Karkotaka, a king among the nagas, and he can't move: a sage's curse has frozen him there until Nala comes to carry him. So the man who lost everything at dice lifts a snake king onto his shoulder and walks out of the fire. And then the snake bites him.
screen: `A VOICE IN THE FIRE.` → `KARKOTAKA, THE SERPENT KING.` → `THEN THE SNAKE BITES HIM.`

segments.voice: Nala's body changes. His beauty is gone. His shape is changed, misshapen, someone no one would look at twice. And Karkotaka explains: I did this so no one will know you. And my poison won't hurt you. It will torment the one who lives inside you, the one who brought all this on you. That's Kali. The bite is a disguise and a medicine at once. Then the serpent gives him a plan. Go to King Rituparna of Ayodhya. Call yourself Vahuka. Offer to drive his horses, because you know horses better than anyone at his court will. And Rituparna knows the secret of dice; he'll teach it to you in exchange. Karkotaka gives him a garment, too: when you want your own shape back, put this on and think of me. So Nala becomes Vahuka, the king's charioteer. He's very good at it. But every evening he says the same lines aloud, a lament for a woman left alone in the forest, wondering where she is. Another servant asks who she is. Nala answers with a story about some foolish man who abandoned his wife, and doesn't say the man is him. Meanwhile, far away, a Brahmana from Vidarbha has found Damayanti at the court of Chedi, and she has gone home to her father's house and her children. She isn't waiting for news. She sends Brahmanas out across the land, to repeat one question in every court and marketplace: where did you go, gambler, after you cut your loving wife's cloth and left her sleeping? And one day, in Ayodhya, a charioteer named Vahuka hears the question, and answers it.
screen: `THE BITE THAT HIDES HIM.` · `NALA BECOMES VAHUKA.` · `A LAMENT EVERY EVENING.` · then, large: `DAMAYANTI SENDS OUT A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle on its own. Nala hides inside a new shape, but every evening the same words come out of him. Notice what your own mind returns to when you're quiet. Don't chase it, and don't push it away. Just let it be there, the way a familiar sound is there in the background of a room. Breathe in, and notice. Breathe out, and let it be. If you pray, you can bring that returning thought into your prayer. If not, simply sit with it kindly. The bell holds the time.
Karkotaka. The naga king whose bite hides Nala and torments Kali inside him, so a king becomes Vahuka the charioteer while a question is sent across the land to find him.
Your line: notice the words you say at day's end. Today, notice the words you say to yourself at day's end, and what they're asking for. Day seven hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: In the Mahabharata's Nala story, the serpent Karkotaka disguises Nala and sends him to serve King Rituparna as the charioteer Vahuka, while Damayanti, back in Vidarbha, sends Brahmanas to search for him.

fork.setup: you're Nala, walking alone after leaving Damayanti. a voice calls your name from a forest fire. what do you do?
options: keep walking; you've got nothing left to give.
follow the voice into the fire.
wait for the fire to burn out.
fork.reveal: he finds the serpent Karkotaka, carries him out, and is bitten, which disguises him and torments Kali.

original.note: Sanskrit Karkotaka, the naga king who disguises Nala with his bite.

trapdoor: what you thought: the snake bit Nala to hurt him.
what it means: the bite hides him and torments Kali, the force that took him over.
what a scholar hears: the poison works on Kali, not on Nala, a step toward the moment Kali has to leave him.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Nalopakhyana: Karkotaka in the fire; the bite; Nala as Vahuka in Rituparna's service; Sudeva finds Damayanti at Chedi; Damayanti sends Brahmanas with her question)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm Karkotaka was cursed (by Narada) to stay motionless until Nala carried him; the sage is left unnamed here.
The text has Karkotaka ask Nala to count his steps and bite him at a particular count (with a wordplay); left out under the claims rule.
Confirm the garment(s) Karkotaka gives to restore Nala's form, and that Rituparna's dice skill is part of the plan.
Damayanti's question is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm its content (the gambler who cut half his wife's cloth and left her sleeping).
Sudeva's recognition of Damayanti (by a mark between her brows) and the queen mother being her aunt are compressed to one sentence.
Editor: review no longer mentions rivers (cut from day 792); 'smaller' changed to 'his shape is changed', since the text describes a changed, deformed form rather than size.
Audit: Karkotaka, the bite, Vahuka in Rituparna's service, the evening verse and Damayanti's question checked; no changes.
